**Group members:** 

Dhriti Iyer (di2251), Michelle Jerry (msj2167), Shaka Ramanathan (sr4354), & Anya Jacoby (abj2136)

**Tentative project title:**

Rats, Rent, and Where to Live: A Data-Driven Apartment Search

**Motivation for this project:**

Next year, we will be graduating with the intention of staying here in New York City! We hope to find a happy home amongst the five boroughs and we'd quite like that home to be rat-free (rat-light if needed). Rats are a common NYC reality, but their distribution varies: we want to use public rodent data to see which neighbourhoods have the biggest and smallest problems, and whether paying more rent actually gets you fewer rats. Then, we will combine that with budget information and commute to find places we want to live in!

**Intended final products:**

A rent vs. rat activity analysis that identifies how neighbourhood affordability intersects with rat prevalence. 

**Anticipated data sources:**

We will use the NYC 311 Service Requests data from NYC Open Data. 311 is New York City’s non-emergency service line, and the dataset includes service requests routed to a city agency for action. Each record is one service request and includes the date and time it was created and closed, the responding agency, the complaint type and descriptor, the location type, the address, the borough-block-lot (BBL) building identifier, and latitude and longitude. In this dataset, rodent complaints are recorded under complaint type “Rodent” and categorized by a descriptor field (e.g. rat sighting, mouse sighting, signs of rodents, conditions attracting rodents).

For NYC rent prices broken down by neighborhood, we will use the StreetEasy Data Dashboard, which is free, publicly available, and updated monthly. It offers neighbourhood-level figures such as median asking rent by borough and neighbourhood, and reflects current market conditions. 

**Planned analyses/Visualizations:**

- Bar chart of complaints by descriptor category
- Interactive map of the concentration of 311 complaints related to rats/rodents, color-coded by neighborhood rent prices
- Month/year heatmap showing seasonality of rat complaints 

**Coding challenges:**

- StreetEasy reports asking rents rather than signed lease prices, so actual rents may be higher or lower.
- Neighborhoods with few listings can produce unstable medians.
- 311 data is not an exhaustive list of all rodent activity as many sightings go unreported or are dealt with by the buildings management and so are not recorded. 
- There is no way to identify specific callers in the data, so we can not distinguish between one person calling about the same thing multiple times or multiple people calling about the same rat problem, so we will need to summarize complaints at the building level rather than using raw counts of complaints.
- The full 311 dataset is very large, so we will need to download only the rodent complaints in batches, which can be done through the NYC Open Data API. Cleaning the data, standardizing variables, and merging with other data sets of interest (average neighborhood rents) will be challenging.
